She had slightly rough skin, a round face, and a flat nose. The Chvostek sign was negative, while the Trousseau sign was positive. Her fourth and fifth metacarpal bones in both hands were shortened, as were the fourth and fifth metatarsal bones in both feet (Figures 3A–D).

Blood tests revealed decreased Ca levels, elevated P, and high PTH levels (Table 2). A head CT scan showed multiple calcifications in the bilateral basal ganglia and frontal cortex (Figure 3E).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Axial non-contrast head CT with red-arrow annotations showing symmetric bilateral basal ganglia calcification in a pseudohypoparathyroidism case (Case 2) from a disease-focused article on pseudohypoparathyroidism; the in-text confirms universal intracranial calcifications with elevated PTH. Real patient imaging of a specific target-disease manifestation; article title states type 1B, so subtype attribution to the configured type 1A key is indirect, lowering confidence. B: Axial non-contrast head CT with red-arrow annotations showing symmetric bilateral cerebellar dentate nucleus calcification, part of the Fahr-pattern intracranial calcification reported universally in the pseudohypoparathyroidism cases of this disease-focused article.
